cases.note: Two equal values sit at different indices, so both are usable.
Negative numbers and a negative target: don't assume the sum grows.
0 + 0 = 0. A check like if (map[need]) would wrongly skip index 0.
The answer is the first and the last element.
The pair is two 5s in the middle.

hints.text: Fix one number x. What would you need to find in the rest of the array, and how quickly can you look a value up?
Scan once while remembering every value you've passed in a hash map (value to index). For each x, check whether target - x is already in the map before you add x.

seen = empty map
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  need = target - nums[i]
  if need is in seen: return [seen[need], i]
  seen[nums[i]] = i

cases.note: One element can't be a duplicate of anything.
0 is falsy: use Set.has, not a truthiness check on a lookup table.
The duplicate is the last pair.
300 values with the only duplicate at the very end: a nested loop gets slow.

hints.text: Do you need to know how many times each value appears, or only whether you have seen it before?
Keep a Set of values seen so far. If the current value is already in it, you're done; otherwise add it. One pass, O(n) time.

seen = empty set
for x in nums:
  if x is in seen: return true
  add x to seen
return false

cases.note: You can't sell before you buy: with one price the profit is 0.
No day is better than another: the answer is 0, not negative.
Buy on day one, sell on the last day.

hints.text: For a fixed selling day, which buying day would you wish you had picked?
Walk left to right, tracking the lowest price seen so far. If you sold today, the profit would be price minus that lowest; keep the maximum of those.

lowest = infinity
best = 0
for p in prices:
  lowest = min(lowest, p)
  best = max(best, p - lowest)
return best

cases.note: Every number is negative: the best subarray is a single element, so don't start 'best' at 0.
A long negative dip: restart instead of carrying the debt.
The best sum is 0, from the lone zero.

hints.text: If you knew the best subarray sum that ends at the previous position, what is the best sum that ends at this one?
Kadane's algorithm: keep the best sum of a subarray ending here. Either extend the previous one or start fresh at this element, whichever is larger, and track the overall maximum.

cur = nums[0]
best = nums[0]
for x in nums[1:]:
  cur = max(x, cur + x)
  best = max(best, cur)
return best

cases.note: No pairs at all.
XOR works on negatives too; a value-to-count table with array indices would not.
The pair is made of zeros.
The single number is 0: a result of 0 must not look like 'not found'.
The single number is last.

hints.text: Every other number comes in a pair. Is there an operation where a value combined with itself cancels out?
XOR has x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, and the order doesn't matter. XOR every number together: the pairs vanish and the single number is left. O(n) time, O(1) space.

result = 0
for x in nums:
  result = result XOR x
return result

cases.note: One number present, so n = 1 and the missing one is 1.
The missing number is 0, the smallest possible.
Everything from 0 to n-1 is present: the missing number is n itself.

hints.text: The numbers should be 0 through n. What would their total be if none were missing?
The sum of 0..n is n * (n + 1) / 2. Subtract the actual sum of the array: the difference is the missing number. (XOR with the indices works too.)

n = length of nums
expected = n * (n + 1) / 2
return expected - sum of nums

cases.note: The majority only shows up after the first element.

hints.text: The majority element appears more than half the time. If you cancelled it against every other element one for one, what would be left standing?
Boyer-Moore voting: keep a candidate and a counter. Same value as the candidate adds one, a different value subtracts one, and at zero you adopt the current value. The majority element survives.

candidate = none; count = 0
for x in nums:
  if count == 0: candidate = x
  if x == candidate: count += 1
  else: count -= 1
return candidate

cases.note: There are no zeros: the array must come back unchanged.
Only zeros.
The only non-zero is last: it has to travel all the way to the front.

hints.text: The non-zero numbers must keep their relative order. Where should the next non-zero number land?
Two pointers: 'write' marks where the next non-zero goes. Scan with 'read'; when nums[read] is non-zero, copy it to write and advance write. Afterwards fill the rest with zeros.

cases.note: Two empty strings are trivially anagrams of each other.
Different lengths: the answer is false before any counting.
Same letters but different counts: a Set-based check wrongly says true.
Same length and letters, different counts.

hints.text: If the two strings have different lengths, can they possibly be anagrams? After that, what do two anagrams have in common?
They contain exactly the same characters with the same counts. Count the characters of s, then subtract while scanning t; any count that goes below zero means t has an extra.

if lengths differ: return false
count = empty map
for c in s: count[c] += 1
for c in t:
  count[c] -= 1
  if count[c] < 0: return false
return true

input: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

cases.note: Only a space: after cleaning there's nothing left, and an empty string is a palindrome.
A and a must match: compare lowercase.
A digit and a letter that look alike are not equal; a regex that drops digits would say true.
Only punctuation.
An underscore is not alphanumeric and must be skipped.

input: Was it a car or a cat I saw?

hints.text: Which characters should count, and what should you do with upper and lower case before comparing?
Two pointers, one at each end. Skip anything that isn't a letter or digit, compare the two lowercase characters, and move both inward. Any mismatch means false.

l = 0; r = length - 1
while l < r:
  skip l forward while s[l] is not alphanumeric
  skip r backward while s[r] is not alphanumeric
  if lowercase(s[l]) != lowercase(s[r]): return false
  l += 1; r -= 1
return true

cases.note: An opener that is never closed: the stack is not empty at the end.
A closer with nothing open: popping an empty stack must not count as a match.
Every bracket has a partner, but they cross instead of nesting.
The right characters in the wrong order.

hints.text: The most recently opened bracket is the first one that has to be closed. Which data structure gives you the latest item first?
Use a stack. Push every opening bracket. On a closing bracket the stack's top must be its matching opener: pop it, otherwise return false. At the end the stack must be empty.

stack = empty
for c in s:
  if c is an opener: push c
  else:
    if stack is empty or top != opener of c: return false
    pop
return stack is empty

cases.note: lo and hi start equal: a loop written as lo < hi never looks at the only element.
The target is the first element: hi = mid - 1 must reach index 0.
The target is the last element.
Bigger than everything: lo walks off the end.
Smaller than everything.
1,000 sorted values: the target is near the end, and (lo + hi) / 2 without flooring breaks.

hints.text: nums is sorted. After comparing the middle element with the target, how much of the array can you throw away?

Keep a window [lo, hi]. Look at mid: if it equals target, done; if it's smaller, the target can only be to the right (lo = mid + 1); otherwise to the left (hi = mid - 1). Stop when the window is empty.

lo = 0; hi = length - 1
while lo <= hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) div 2
  if nums[mid] == target: return mid
  if nums[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
  else: hi = mid - 1
return -1

cases.note: One step: there is exactly one way, and a loop starting at i = 2 never runs.
Plain recursion makes over a million calls here and times out.
The largest n the constraints allow: about 1.8 billion ways, still exact in a double.

hints.text: To stand on step n, which two steps could your last move have started from?
ways(n) = ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2): a Fibonacci recurrence. Computing it recursively repeats work exponentially, so build it up from the bottom and keep only the last two values.

a = 1; b = 1
repeat n - 1 times:
  next = a + b
  a = b
  b = next
return b

cases.note: One string: it is its own longest common prefix.
An empty string in the list forces an empty answer.
Every string is identical: the whole string is the prefix.
The shorter string is itself the prefix: don't index past its end.
Same pair in the other order.

hints.text: The common prefix can never be longer than the shortest string. How can you check one column of characters across all the strings?
Take the first string as the candidate. Compare it with each other string and shorten the candidate until that string starts with it. If the candidate becomes empty, stop early.

cases.note: One symbol: there's no 'next' symbol to compare against.
A smaller symbol before a bigger one is subtracted: 4, not 6.
Two subtractive pairs back to back.
3999, the largest numeral in the constraints.

hints.text: Each symbol has a fixed value. When is a symbol's value added, and when does a smaller symbol in front of a bigger one change that?
Scan left to right. If the current symbol is smaller than the one right after it (IV, IX, XL ...), subtract it; otherwise add it.

cases.note: 9 + 1 = 10: the result is longer than the input.
[0] + 1 = [1]: no carry, and it must not be mistaken for an empty or falsy number.
The carry runs through every digit and a new leading 1 is needed.
100 nines: turning the digits into a Number loses precision, so work digit by digit.

hints.text: Think about adding 1 by hand, starting at the rightmost digit. When does the addition stop mattering for the digits to the left?
Walk from the last digit to the first. A digit below 9 just goes up by one and you're done; a 9 becomes 0 and the carry moves left. If you fall off the front, the answer is a 1 followed by all zeros.

cases.note: 1 is already happy: the loop must not run before the first check.
4 enters the loop 4, 16, 37, 58, 89, 145, 42, 20, 4: without repeat detection this never ends.
The largest 32-bit value: digit extraction with string or number tricks must cope with 10 digits.

hints.text: Try a few starting numbers by hand. After repeating the process enough times, what kinds of things can happen to the sequence?
Either you reach 1 or the sequence repeats forever. Detect a repeat with a set of values already seen, or with two pointers moving at different speeds (slow and fast, like cycle detection in a list).

seen = empty set
while n != 1 and n is not in seen:
  add n to seen
  n = sum of the squares of the digits of n
return n == 1

cases.note: The only word is the empty string: it still forms its own group, [[""]].
Identical words are anagrams of each other and all stay in the result.
No two words are anagrams: every group holds exactly one word.
300 short words: re-checking every word against every group with a sort per comparison is slow; hash by a key instead.

hints.text: What do two anagrams have in common that you can compute for each word on its own, without comparing pairs of words?
Give every word a canonical key: its letters sorted, or its 26 letter counts. Words with the same key are anagrams, so bucket them in a hash map from key to list of words.

groups = empty map from key to list
for word in strs:
  key = letters of word sorted
  append word to groups[key]
return all the lists in groups

cases.note: One value, k = 1: the answer is that value.
Only one distinct value exists.
k equals the number of distinct values: every value, including the rarest, is in the answer.
Negative values: a frequency table indexed by the value itself breaks.
The most frequent value is 0, which is falsy.
Any order of the k values is accepted; the answer is the set {1, 2}.
465 numbers where value v appears v times (1..30): sorting every pair or rescanning for each value is the slow route.

hints.text: Counting how often each value appears is the first step. Once you have the counts, what is left is choosing the k biggest.

Build a frequency map. Then either sort the distinct values by count, or bucket values by their count (a value appears at most n times) and read buckets from the highest count down until you have k values.

cases.note: Each answer is just the other number.
Two zeros make every product 0. Dividing the total by nums[i] would divide by zero.
Exactly one zero: only that position gets a non-zero answer.
1000 numbers: recomputing the product for every index is O(n^2).

hints.text: For position i the answer is (everything to its left) times (everything to its right). Can you get either side cheaply for every i?

Make one pass left to right storing the running product of everything before each index, then one pass right to left multiplying in the running product of everything after it. No division, O(n) time, O(1) extra space beyond the output.

result = list of n ones
prefix = 1
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  result[i] = prefix
  prefix = prefix * nums[i]
suffix = 1
for i from n - 1 down to 0:
  result[i] = result[i] * suffix
  suffix = suffix * nums[i]
return result

cases.note: No numbers, no run: the answer is 0.
The repeated 1 must not extend the run: 0, 1, 2 has length 3, not 4.
Only one distinct value: the answer is 1.
Huge spread of values rules out a count array indexed by value.
A shuffled run 0..1199: sorting is fine, but rescanning the array for every next value is far too slow.

hints.text: Sorting makes this easy but costs O(n log n). If you could test 'is x in the array' instantly, where would you start counting a run?

Put everything in a hash set. A number begins a run only if its predecessor (x - 1) is absent. From each start, walk x + 1, x + 2, ... while they are in the set and track the longest run. Every element is visited a constant number of times.

cases.note: A single row, [[1]]: loops that fill inner entries never run.
Two rows, all ones: there is no inner entry to compute yet, so row r - 1 must not be indexed past its end.
30 rows with values up to 77 million: a recursive entry-by-entry formula without memoising explodes.

hints.text: Write out the first five rows by hand. How is each inner number related to the row right above it?

Each row starts and ends with 1. Every inner entry is the sum of the two entries directly above it (the one above-left and the one above-right). Build the triangle one row at a time from the previous row.

triangle = empty list
for r from 0 to numRows - 1:
  row = list of r + 1 ones
  for c from 1 to r - 1:
    row[c] = triangle[r - 1][c - 1] + triangle[r - 1][c]
  append row to triangle
return triangle

cases.note: nums2 is empty: nothing to merge, nums1 must stay as it is.
nums1 holds no real elements: its single 0 is just free space, not a value to merge.
Real zeros in nums1 and nums2 alongside the padding zeros: count by m and n, never by value.
Every element of nums2 goes before every element of nums1.
500 + 500 interleaved values: shifting elements right on every insert is quadratic.

hints.text: nums1 has free room at its end. If you merged from the front you would overwrite values you still need. Which end is safe to fill first?

Fill from the back. Use three pointers: the last real element of nums1, the last element of nums2, and the write position at the very end of nums1. Place the larger of the two candidates there and move that pointer and the write pointer left. When nums2 runs out, you are done.

i = m - 1
j = n - 1
w = m + n - 1
while j >= 0:
  if i >= 0 and nums1[i] > nums2[j]:
    nums1[w] = nums1[i]
    i -= 1
  else:
    nums1[w] = nums2[j]
    j -= 1
  w -= 1

cases.note: k = 0: nothing moves.
One element: any k leaves it in place, and k mod 1 is 0.
k equals the length: a full turn, so the array is unchanged. Handle it without a negative or zero-length reversal.
k is larger than the array: only k mod n matters (5 mod 3 = 2).
k = 99999 on 1500 numbers: rotating one step at a time, k times, is far too slow; take k mod n.

hints.text: Rotating right by k moves the last k elements to the front. What happens when k is bigger than the array, or a multiple of its length?
Reduce k to k mod n first. Then reverse the whole array, reverse the first k elements, and reverse the remaining n - k elements. Three reversals do the rotation in place with O(1) extra space.

k = k mod n
reverse nums from index 0 to n - 1
reverse nums from index 0 to k - 1
reverse nums from index k to n - 1

cases.note: Only one colour: no swaps are needed.
Already in order: a pointer that swaps blindly can still scramble it.
All 2s sit before all 0s: every element crosses the whole array.
After swapping a 2 to the back, the value that arrives at mid has to be checked again.

hints.text: There are only three distinct values. What does that let you do that a general sort cannot?

Dutch national flag: keep three regions, 0s on the left, 2s on the right, 1s in the middle, with a scan pointer in the unknown part. A 0 swaps to the left boundary, a 2 swaps to the right boundary (and is re-examined), a 1 just advances.

cases.note: The single element is itself the matching subarray: the empty prefix (sum 0) must be counted.
Every one of the 6 subarrays sums to 0: counting must handle many equal prefix sums.
Negatives let a window shrink and grow: a sliding window gives wrong counts here.
No subarray adds up to k: the answer is 0.
Three overlapping windows match: overlapping subarrays all count.
1500 numbers: checking every subarray sum from scratch is cubic and times out.

hints.text: A subarray's sum is the difference of two prefix sums. For the prefix ending at index j, which earlier prefix sum would make the difference exactly k?

Walk once, keeping a running prefix sum and a hash map from prefix-sum value to how many times it has occurred (seed it with 0 occurring once). At each step, add the count of (prefix - k) to the answer, then record the current prefix. This works with negatives, unlike a sliding window.

counts = map with {0: 1}
prefix = 0
answer = 0
for x in nums:
  prefix += x
  answer += counts[prefix - k] (0 if absent)
  counts[prefix] += 1
return answer

cases.note: Already standing on the last index: true, even though the jump length is 0.
A zero at the start with somewhere to go: stuck, so false.
The first jump lands on a zero that can never move on.
The jump lands exactly on the last index, hopping over a zero.
A jump far longer than needed: don't index past the end.
60 positions: trying every jump length recursively without memoisation is exponential here, and the answer is false.

hints.text: You don't need the actual path, only whether the last index can be reached. If you know one index is reachable, which indices become reachable because of it?

Track the farthest index reachable so far while scanning left to right. If the scan reaches an index beyond the farthest reach, you are stuck and the answer is false. If the farthest reach ever covers the last index, it is true.

farthest = 0
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  if i > farthest: return false
  farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])
  if farthest >= n - 1: return true
return true

cases.note: Only one pair exists, and the answer is 1-indexed: [1, 2], not [0, 1].
Two zeros sum to 0. A truthiness check on a lookup would skip them.
Negative values and a negative target: the sum gets larger as you move right.
The answer is the very first and the very last element.
The pair is two equal 4s next to each other.
2 + 2 = 4 tempts you to use the middle element twice. The answer is 1 and 3.
1500 values with the answer at the far end: trying every pair is slow.

hints.text: The array is already sorted. If the sum of two chosen numbers is too big, which of the two would you move, and in which direction?

Two pointers from both ends. A sum above target means the right value is too large, so move the right pointer in; a sum below target means move the left pointer out. O(n) time, O(1) space. Remember the answer is 1-indexed.

left = 0
right = n - 1
while left < right:
  sum = numbers[left] + numbers[right]
  if sum == target: return [left + 1, right + 1]
  if sum < target: left += 1
  else: right -= 1

cases.note: Three zeros make exactly one triplet, not one per way of choosing them.
Three numbers is the smallest legal input: the loop over the first value runs once.
Many zeros still give a single [0,0,0]. Without skipping repeats you list it many times.
Two 2s and two 0s: [-2,0,2] must be reported once, not four times.
No triple sums to zero: return an empty list.
Zeros give two different triplets: [0,0,0] and [-1,0,1].
2400 zeros plus -1 and 1: a triple loop does billions of steps and repeat-skipping matters.

hints.text: If you fix one number, what is left to find in the rest of the array? And how would sorting help you avoid listing the same triplet twice?

Sort first. For each distinct first value, run the two-pointer search for a pair that sums to its negation on the remainder. After a hit, skip over repeated values on both pointers so each triplet appears once.

sort nums
for i from 0 to n - 3:
  if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]: continue
  left = i + 1, right = n - 1
  while left < right:
    sum = nums[i] + nums[left] + nums[right]
    if sum < 0: left += 1
    else if sum > 0: right -= 1
    else: record triplet, move both pointers, skip repeated values

cases.note: A wall of height 0 holds nothing: the area is 0, not negative or the other height.
Ties everywhere: the widest pair (width 4) wins.
The best pair is the two outer walls.
Max heights with zeros between them: 10000 * 4 = 40000.
1500 pseudo-random walls: checking every pair is about a million steps and grows quickly.

hints.text: The area is limited by the shorter wall times the distance between the walls. Which choice gives you the widest start, and what do you give up when you shrink it?
Start with the outermost pair. Moving the taller wall inward can only shrink the width without raising the limit, so always move the shorter wall inward and keep the best area seen.

left = 0
right = n - 1
best = 0
while left < right:
  area = min(height[left], height[right]) * (right - left)
  best = max(best, area)
  if height[left] < height[right]: left += 1
  else: right -= 1
return best

cases.note: One negative number: the result is just [9].
All negative: squaring reverses the order, so the biggest square comes from the left end.
Equal absolute values from both sides: either pointer may go first, the output is the same.
Squares reach 100,000,000: fine for numbers, but check any fixed-size assumptions.
Non-negative input: squares are already in order.
1500 values mixing both signs: a merge or two-pointer pass is linear, re-sorting is not.

hints.text: Squaring wrecks the order when there are negatives. Where in the original array can the largest square ever be?

The largest square is at one of the two ends. Use two pointers on the ends and fill the result from the back: compare absolute values, write the bigger square, and move that pointer inward. O(n), no sort needed.

cases.note: One character: the pointers start equal, nothing to swap.
Reversing leaves it unchanged. A solution that only prints would still look right here.
A single swap with no middle element.
Upper and lower case, a digit and a symbol: swap characters as they are, don't change case.
1500 characters, to be reversed in place without building a new array.

hints.text: What has to happen to the first and last items, then the second and second-to-last, and so on? When do you stop?
Two pointers, one at each end. Swap the pair they point at and move them toward each other until they meet or cross. No extra array is needed, so space is O(1).

left = 0
right = n - 1
while left < right:
  swap s[left] and s[right]
  left += 1
  right -= 1

cases.note: Dropping either end still leaves a non-palindrome. Return false instead of falling off the loop.
Delete either letter and one remains: true.
4001 characters with the only fix at the very end: re-checking from scratch per character is quadratic.

hints.text: Walk inward from both ends as in a normal palindrome check. What should happen at the first pair that does not match?

At the first mismatch you get one deletion: either drop the left character or the right one. Check whether the remaining inner string is a palindrome for either choice; if neither works the answer is false.

cases.note: The empty string has no substring: the answer is 0, so don't read s[0].
No repeats at all: the whole string is the answer.
When the last 'a' is seen, its old index is outside the window. Moving the left edge back to it gives 4 instead of 2.
Upper and lower case differ, and spaces and symbols count as characters too.
5200 characters: re-scanning each window from scratch is far slower than a single pass.

hints.text: If the current stretch has no repeats and you add one more character that does repeat, where must the stretch now begin?

Sliding window with a map from character to its last seen index. When the new character was last seen inside the window, jump the left edge to just past that index (never backwards). Track the biggest window.

last = empty map
left = 0
best = 0
for right from 0 to n - 1:
  if s[right] in last and last[s[right]] >= left:
    left = last[s[right]] + 1
  last[s[right]] = right
  best = max(best, right - left + 1)
return best

cases.note: k = 0 allows no replacements: the answer is the longest run of one letter (here 1).
Nothing needs replacing and k is spare: the answer is the full length, not length + k.
k equals the length: every letter can change, but the answer is still capped at the string length.
3000 characters: counting every substring from scratch is cubic.

hints.text: For a chosen stretch of the string, how many replacements do you need to make all letters the same? Which letter should you keep?

A window is valid when its length minus the count of its most frequent letter is at most k. Slide a window: grow the right edge, and when it becomes invalid, move the left edge once. Track the best length.

counts = empty map
left = 0
maxFreq = 0
best = 0
for right from 0 to n - 1:
  counts[s[right]] += 1
  maxFreq = max(maxFreq, counts[s[right]])
  while (right - left + 1) - maxFreq > k:
    counts[s[left]] -= 1
    left += 1
  best = max(best, right - left + 1)
return best

cases.note: One-letter s1: a match is just that letter appearing in s2.
s1 is longer than s2, so no window fits. Don't index past the end.
The whole of s2 is the window, and it is the reverse of s1.
The permutation sits in the last window: make sure the final slide is checked.
s1 has two a's: counts must match exactly, not just 'the same set of letters'.
A 100-letter s1 and a 1600-letter s2: rebuilding counts from scratch per window is slow.

hints.text: Two strings are permutations of each other exactly when their letter counts are identical. How long should each stretch of s2 you examine be?

Slide a window of length s1.length across s2, maintaining letter counts incrementally: add the new right letter, remove the old left letter. Compare the counts of the window with those of s1 (or track how many letters match).

if len(s1) > len(s2): return false
need = counts of letters in s1
window = counts of the first len(s1) letters of s2
if window == need: return true
for right from len(s1) to len(s2) - 1:
  add s2[right] to window
  remove s2[right - len(s1)] from window
  if window == need: return true
return false

cases.note: s has only one 'a' but t needs two: return the empty string.
t needs two A's, so the window must stretch to cover both. Counts matter, not just the set of letters.
Every window of length 2 is the same string. Return it, not the whole thing.
Case matters: 'A' and 'a' are different letters, so the lowercase 'a' at the front doesn't count.
The only minimum window ends at the last character.
A 2400-character string: the shortest window is at the very end, after long misleading windows.

hints.text: A stretch of s works when it holds every letter of t with enough copies. Once a stretch works, can you make it shorter from the left?

Sliding window with a need-count per letter and a counter of how many requirements are satisfied. Grow right until all are met, then shrink left as long as they stay met, recording the shortest window each time.

need = counts of letters in t, missing = len(t)
left = 0, best = none
for right from 0 to n - 1:
  if need[s[right]] > 0: missing -= 1
  need[s[right]] -= 1
  while missing == 0:
    keep window left..right if shortest so far
    need[s[left]] += 1
    if need[s[left]] > 0: missing += 1
    left += 1
return best, or empty string

cases.note: p is longer than s: return an empty list without reading past the end.
Matches overlap: every start from 0 to 3 counts.
The only match starts at the last possible index (4).
3000 characters with a match at every tenth position: comparing sorted windows is slow, and indices must stay ascending.

hints.text: Which stretches of s could possibly be an anagram of p, and what is the one thing about letters that makes two strings anagrams?

Anagrams have equal letter counts. Slide a window of length p.length across s, update the counts by adding the new letter and removing the old one, and record the start index whenever the counts equal p's counts.

if len(p) > len(s): return empty list
need = counts of letters in p
window = counts of the first len(p) letters of s
result = empty list
if window == need: add 0 to result
for right from len(p) to len(s) - 1:
  add s[right] to window
  remove s[right - len(p)] from window
  if window == need: add (right - len(p) + 1) to result
return result

cases.note: The empty string is a subsequence of anything: return true without scanning.
s is longer than t, so it can never fit.
Both empty: still true.
Each letter of t is used at most once: three a's are needed but t has only two.
The match uses the first and the last character of t.
1200 letters against 3000: a full 2D table or recursion over both strings is far heavier than one scan.

hints.text: Read t from left to right. What is the next letter of s you are still waiting to see?
Two pointers: one into s (next letter needed) and one scanning t. Advance the s pointer only when the letters match. s is a subsequence exactly when the s pointer reaches the end.

cases.note: There is no later day, so the answer is just [0].
Equal is not warmer: every day waits forever, so all zeros.
Nothing is ever warmer than what came before, so every answer is 0.
Values at both limits, with ties at 100 that must not count as warmer.
Repeated 60s: a tie must stay on the stack until something strictly warmer arrives.
1500 days of repeating long cold stretches: re-scanning forward for every day is quadratic.

hints.text: When you reach a warm day, which of the earlier days were still waiting for something warmer than themselves?
Keep a stack of day indices whose answer is still unknown; their temperatures never increase from bottom to top. Each new day resolves (pops) every waiting day that is colder, and then waits itself.

answer = array of zeros, same length as temperatures
waiting = empty stack of indices
for i from 0 to n - 1:
  while waiting is not empty and temperatures[top of waiting] < temperatures[i]:
    j = pop waiting
    answer[j] = i - j
  push i onto waiting
return answer

cases.note: A lone number token is already the answer: no operator ever runs.
-7 / 2 must give -3 (truncate toward zero), not -4 from Math.floor.
A zero operand with subtraction: the operand order (left minus right) decides the sign.
Negative divisor: the quotient -3.5 truncates to -3, and the token '-2' is a number, not an operator.
The largest operands, ending near 1.6 billion: still inside 32 bits but easy to bungle with bitwise tricks.
1200+ tokens, one long left-leaning chain: a recursive parser nests very deep, and re-scanning for operators is slow.

hints.text: When you meet an operator, which two values does it apply to, and where have those values been waiting?

Use a stack of numbers. Push each number token. For an operator, pop the right operand first, then the left one, apply the operator, and push the result. Division must truncate toward zero, not floor.

stack = empty
for token in tokens:
  if token is a number: push its integer value
  else:
    right = pop stack
    left = pop stack
    push (left token right), truncating division toward zero
return the only value left on the stack

cases.note: n = 1 has exactly one answer, '()': loops that assume at least two pairs break.
Two answers, '(())' and '()()'. Any order is accepted, so don't rely on one.
429 results. Generating all 2^14 strings and filtering wastes work; pruning keeps only valid prefixes.

hints.text: At each position you choose '(' or ')'. What simple rule keeps the prefix from ever becoming impossible to fix?

Backtracking: keep counts of opens and closes used so far. You may add '(' while opens < n, and add ')' only while closes < opens. Every string that reaches length 2n is valid, so no final check is needed.

results = empty list
build(current, opens, closes):
  if length of current == 2 * n: add current to results; return
  if opens < n: build(current + '(', opens + 1, closes)
  if closes < opens: build(current + ')', opens, closes + 1)
build('', 0, 0)
return results

cases.note: One bar of width 1: the area is simply its height.
Equal heights: the whole histogram is one rectangle, so equal bars must be merged, not split.
Heights only rise, so nothing is popped until the end: a final flush is required.
A zero-height bar splits the histogram: the best rectangle can't span it.
Every bar has height 0, so the answer is 0 (not undefined or -Infinity).
Max heights: the area is 30000 and must come from the width times the height.
1200 strictly rising bars: an O(n^2) scan does about 700k steps here, the stack version does about 2400.

hints.text: For one bar to be the shortest bar of a rectangle, how far can that rectangle stretch to the left and to the right?

Maintain a stack of bar indices with increasing heights. When a bar is lower than the stack top, the top bar can no longer extend right, so pop it and compute its area: its width runs from the new top of the stack (exclusive) to the current index (exclusive). Add a final height-0 bar to flush the stack.

stack = empty (indices, heights increasing)
best = 0
for i from 0 to n (treat height at index n as 0):
  while stack not empty and height[top] >= height at i:
    h = height[pop]
    leftEdge = (stack empty) ? 0 : top + 1
    best = max(best, h * (i - leftEdge))
  push i
return best

cases.note: Nothing follows the only element, so the answer is [-1].
Every value's next greater is the very next element, except the last, which has none.
A strictly falling nums2 has no greater element anywhere to the right, so all -1.
The element sits at the very end of nums2: no greater value can come after it.
0 is a real value: a map lookup using truthiness would treat a stored 0 as missing.
Values at both limits of the range.
1000 distinct values in nums2: rescanning to the right for each lookup is quadratic work.

hints.text: Forget nums1 for a moment: how would you find the next greater value for every element of nums2 in one pass?

Walk nums2 with a stack of values still waiting for a bigger one. Each new value pops (and answers) every smaller waiting value; record 'value to its next greater' in a map. Then answer each nums1 entry with a map lookup, defaulting to -1.

cases.note: No brackets at all: plain letters must pass through untouched.
The shortest encoded string: a repeat count of 1 around one letter.
The maximum repeat count (300) with a two-letter body: three digits and a 600-character result.
800 levels of nesting: recursion that does too much per level, or builds strings badly, struggles here.

hints.text: When you hit ']', what do you need to remember from the matching '[' to finish the repeat?

Use a stack. Keep the text built so far and the repeat count being read (counts can have several digits). On '[', push both and start fresh. On ']', pop the previous text and count, then set current = previous + current repeated count times.

stack = empty
current = empty text
count = 0
for ch in s:
  if ch is a digit: count = count * 10 + digit
  else if ch == '[': push (current, count); current = empty; count = 0
  else if ch == ']': (prev, k) = pop; current = prev + current repeated k times
  else: append ch to current
return current

cases.note: Bigger than everything: the answer is nums.length, one past the last index.
One element and a smaller target: insert at the front, index 0.
Smaller than everything: the answer is 0.
Both ends of the allowed range, with the target equal to the maximum.
1000 sorted values and a target that is absent: a linear scan works but binary search needs about 10 steps.

hints.text: If target isn't in the array, which position is 'the first element that is not smaller than target'?

Binary search for the lower bound: the smallest index whose value is >= target (or n if none). That index is both the match position and the insertion position. Use a half-open range [lo, hi) with hi = n so the 'append at the end' answer is reachable.

lo = 0
hi = length of nums
while lo < hi:
  mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2, rounded down
  if nums[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
  else: hi = mid
return lo

cases.note: sqrt(0) is 0: a search that starts at lo = 1 or divides by mid breaks here.
The smallest positive input is its own root.
46340 squared exactly. Squaring a guess above that overflows a 32-bit int.
The largest 32-bit value: counting up one by one takes tens of thousands of steps, and mid * mid overflows in 32-bit math.

hints.text: The answer is the largest integer r whose square does not exceed x. What kind of search finds 'the largest value that still satisfies a test'?

Binary search r between 0 and x (or a tighter cap). If mid * mid <= x, mid is a candidate and the answer is mid or larger; otherwise search lower. Compare mid * mid with x directly, or use mid <= x / mid, instead of calling a built-in square root.

lo = 0
hi = min(x, 46340)
answer = 0
while lo <= hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2, rounded down
  if mid * mid <= x:
    answer = mid
    lo = mid + 1
  else:
    hi = mid - 1
return answer

cases.note: One pile of 7 in 3 hours: ceil(7 / k) <= 3 first holds at k = 3.
h equals the number of piles, so each pile gets exactly one hour: speed 5.
h equals the pile count: Koko must finish a pile every hour, so the speed is the largest pile.
A huge h: the minimum speed floors at 1, never 0.
A pile of 1 billion: the answer is 500000000, and a speed-by-speed scan from 1 would take forever.
800 piles and thousands of candidate speeds: recomputing hours for every speed from 1 is slow; binary search is not.

hints.text: If someone handed you a speed k, how would you decide whether it finishes in h hours? And what happens to that answer as k grows?

Feasibility is monotonic: if speed k works, any faster speed works too. Binary search the speed between 1 and the biggest pile. For a candidate speed, the hours needed are the sum over piles of ceil(pile / k).

lo = 1
hi = largest pile
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2, rounded down
  hours = sum over piles of ceil(pile / mid)
  if hours <= h: hi = mid
  else: lo = mid + 1
return lo

cases.note: A one-element array is its own minimum: the loop should not run at all.
The smallest array that is actually rotated: mid equals lo, so mid + 1 matters.
Rotated n times, i.e. not rotated at all: the minimum is the first element.
The minimum is the last element, the largest possible rotation shift.
The minimum is 0: a result of 0 must not be mistaken for 'not found'.
1000 rotated values: fine for a full scan, but the intent is O(log n).

hints.text: Compare the middle element with the last one. Which half must contain the drop (the minimum)?

Binary search with lo and hi. If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the minimum is strictly to the right of mid, so lo = mid + 1. Otherwise the minimum is at mid or to its left, so hi = mid. When lo meets hi you are on the minimum; no special case for 'not rotated'.

lo = 0
hi = length of nums - 1
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2, rounded down
  if nums[mid] > nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1
  else: hi = mid
return nums[lo]

cases.note: One element that isn't the target: the answer is -1, and the loop must still terminate.
Two elements, rotated: mid equals lo, so 'which half is sorted' must use <=, not <.
Not rotated at all: the usual binary search must still work.
The target is the first element, which sits on the 'big' side of the rotation.
The target is the last element.
The target is larger than every value: return -1, don't return mid or lo.
800 rotated values and a target near the middle of the sorted order: the intent is O(log n).

hints.text: Cut the array at the middle: is one of the two halves always fully sorted? How could you tell which one?

In each step, at least one half around mid is sorted. Compare nums[lo] with nums[mid] to find it, then check whether target lies inside that sorted half's range. If it does, search that half; otherwise search the other one.

lo = 0
hi = length of nums - 1
while lo <= hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2, rounded down
  if nums[mid] == target: return mid
  if nums[lo] <= nums[mid]:
    if nums[lo] <= target and target < nums[mid]: hi = mid - 1
    else: lo = mid + 1
  else:
    if nums[mid] < target and target <= nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid - 1
return -1

cases.note: A 1x1 matrix with an absent target: row and column bounds collapse to a single cell.
A single row where the target is the last cell: the bottom-right corner.
The very last cell of the matrix.
The very first cell of the matrix.
24 falls inside the numeric range of the last row but isn't there: only a full check rules it out.
A 30x30 grid: scanning every cell works but the sorted layout allows about 10 comparisons.

hints.text: Rows are sorted and each row starts after the previous one ends. If you wrote all the rows end to end, what would you have?
The matrix behaves like one sorted array of m * n values. Binary search over indices 0 .. m * n - 1 and map an index back to a cell with row = floor(index / n) and column = index mod n.

rows = number of rows
cols = number of columns
lo = 0
hi = rows * cols - 1
while lo <= hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2, rounded down
  value = matrix[mid / cols, rounded down][mid mod cols]
  if value == target: return true
  if value < target: lo = mid + 1
  else: hi = mid - 1
return false

cases.note: With one house there is no neighbour to conflict with: take it.
Every house ties: the answer is two houses, not all four and not one.
You can only take one of two adjacent houses: the answer is the larger, not the sum.
Skipping two houses in a row to reach both big values beats alternating greedily.
100 houses: trying every take/skip combination is exponential and never finishes.

hints.text: Standing at house i, you either take its cash or you don't. What does each choice tell you about house i - 1?

Let best(i) be the most you can collect from the first i houses. Taking house i forces you to skip i - 1, so best(i) is the larger of best(i - 1) and best(i - 2) plus nums[i]. Only the last two values are ever needed.

prev2 = 0
prev1 = 0
for x in nums:
  take = prev2 + x
  skip = prev1
  prev2 = prev1
  prev1 = max(take, skip)
return prev1

cases.note: Only even totals are reachable with a 2-coin: return -1, not Infinity or 0.
Amount 0 needs zero coins. It is not -1 and not 1.
One coin denomination that matches the amount exactly.
Every coin is even and the amount is odd, so nothing reaches it.
The coin is bigger than the amount: no coin fits. Watch for overflow-style sentinels.
Amount 6249 with awkward coins: trying every coin sequence recursively explodes.

hints.text: If you always grab the biggest coin that fits, can you find a coin set where that goes wrong?

Define fewest(a) as the minimum coins to make amount a. Try every coin c as the last coin used: fewest(a) = 1 + the best of fewest(a - c). Build it up from 0, treating unreachable amounts as infinity.

cases.note: The subsequence must be strictly increasing, so equal values never chain: the answer is 1.
The whole array is the answer: every element extends the chain.
No two elements increase: the answer is 1.
Repeated 4s must not both be used; an equal value should replace a tail, not extend it.
500 scrambled values: trying every subsequence is 2^500, and even the O(n^2) table is the slow route.

hints.text: If you fix the last element of an increasing subsequence, what do you need to know about everything before it?

For each position, the best length ending there is 1 plus the best among earlier, strictly smaller values (O(n^2)). For O(n log n), keep the smallest possible tail for each length and binary-search where the current value belongs.

tails = empty list
for x in nums:
  find the first index k in tails with tails[k] >= x (binary search)
  if no such index: append x to tails
  else: tails[k] = x
return length of tails

cases.note: No shared characters: the answer is 0, not undefined.
Identical strings: the whole string is the common subsequence.
Repeated letters: each character of the shorter string can be used only once.
Two 300-character strings: plain recursion without memoisation repeats the same pairs exponentially often.

hints.text: Compare the last characters of the two strings. What can you conclude if they match, and what if they don't?

Let L(i, j) be the answer for the first i characters of one string and the first j of the other. A match gives 1 + L(i - 1, j - 1); a mismatch gives the larger of L(i - 1, j) and L(i, j - 1). Fill a table.

cases.note: Turning an empty word into abc takes exactly 3 inserts: the base row of the table.
One replacement, which is cheaper than a delete plus an insert.
The mirror case: 3 deletes to reach the empty word.
Both words empty: nothing to do, answer 0.
Identical words need 0 edits.
Two 200-character words: unmemoised recursion branches three ways per mismatch and never finishes.

hints.text: Look only at the last characters of both words. If they are equal you can ignore them. If not, what three moves could fix the mismatch?

Let D(i, j) be the edits to turn the first i letters of word1 into the first j of word2. On a mismatch take 1 plus the smallest of D(i - 1, j) (delete), D(i, j - 1) (insert) and D(i - 1, j - 1) (replace). The base cases are an empty prefix on either side.

cases.note: Start and finish are the same cell: one path, with no moves at all.
A single row has exactly one path; a table that starts at row 1 may skip the base case.
A tall single column at the maximum height: still exactly one path.
A 17x17 grid has over 600 million paths: counting them one by one with plain recursion times out.

hints.text: To reach a cell you must have come from exactly two neighbours. How many ways are there to reach the cells along the top row and left column?
paths(r, c) = paths(r - 1, c) + paths(r, c - 1), with 1 for any cell in the first row or column. You only need one row of the table at a time.

cases.note: Greedy splitting finds cats + and, then gets stuck on og: only trying every split point answers false.
Dictionary words can be used any number of times.
Words of length 3 and 4 overlap: taking the 4 first leaves 3 letters, which only works if the remainder is checked, not assumed.
Every split of the a's works until the final b fails: unmemoised recursion tries exponentially many splits.

hints.text: If a prefix of s is a dictionary word, what is left to figure out about the remaining suffix?
Let ok[i] mean the first i characters can be split into words. ok[i] is true when some earlier ok[j] is true and s[j..i) is a word. Put the words in a set for O(1) lookups.

cases.note: A leading zero is not a valid code, and 06 is not 6: the answer is 0.
A lone 0 has no letter: return 0, not 1.
The 0 only works glued to the 1: exactly one decoding, not two.
10 then a stranded 0, or 1 then 00: neither works, so the answer is 0.
27 is above 26, so it can only be split as 2 and 7.
Forty-five 1s give over 1.8 billion decodings: recursion without memoisation never finishes.

hints.text: Look at the last one or two digits of the string. When is each of those a valid letter code?
Let ways[i] count decodings of the first i digits. A single digit 1-9 adds ways[i - 1]; a two-digit number from 10 to 26 adds ways[i - 2]. A zero can only be used as part of 10 or 20.

ways[0] = 1
ways[1] = 0 if s[0] is 0, else 1
for i from 2 to length of s:
  ways[i] = 0
  if s[i - 1] is not 0: ways[i] += ways[i - 1]
  two = number made by s[i - 2] and s[i - 1]
  if two is between 10 and 26: ways[i] += ways[i - 2]
return ways[length of s]

cases.note: The zero splits the array: the best answer is 0, not -2 and not 2.
One negative number: the answer is that number, so don't start the best at 0 or 1.
All negative: the best is the last two, product 1; a running max alone says 3 or -1.
1500 values of mostly 1 and -1 with sparse 2s and zeros: an all-subarrays product loop does over a million multiplications.

hints.text: Why isn't tracking only the best product ending at each index enough once negative numbers appear?
A very negative product can become the biggest after multiplying by another negative. Track both the largest and the smallest product of a subarray ending at the current element. A zero resets both.

best = nums[0]
high = nums[0]
low = nums[0]
for x in nums[1:]:
  candidates = [x, high * x, low * x]
  high = max of candidates
  low = min of candidates
  best = max(best, high)
return best

cases.note: The total is 11, which is odd, so an equal split cannot exist.
One element can never be split into two equal halves.
The total is even (8) but no subset reaches 4: parity alone is not enough.
100 numbers with an even total but no valid split: trying every subset is hopeless, a reachable-sums table is quick.

hints.text: If the two halves must be equal, what does that say about the total sum, and what single number are you aiming for?
Let target be half the total (an odd total is an instant no). The question becomes: can some subset reach exactly target? Track which sums are reachable, adding one number at a time.

total = sum of nums
if total is odd: return false
target = total / 2
reachable[0] = true, all other sums false
for x in nums:
  for s from target down to x:
    if reachable[s - x]: reachable[s] = true
return reachable[target]

cases.note: No set bits: the loop must not run, and the answer is 0.
All 32 bits set: with signed shifts this becomes -1 and an arithmetic >> loop never ends.
Only bit 31 is set. It is the sign bit in 32-bit signed math, so n & 1 and >> misbehave.
The smallest positive value has a single set bit in the lowest position.

hints.text: What does n & 1 tell you, and how can you move on to the next bit?

Either shift right one bit at a time counting the low bit, or use n & (n - 1), which clears the lowest set bit so the loop runs once per set bit. Remember JavaScript bitwise operators work on signed 32-bit values.

n = n as an unsigned 32-bit value
count = 0
while n is not 0:
  count = count + (n AND 1)
  n = n shifted right by 1 (unsigned shift)
return count

cases.note: n = 0 still returns an array with one entry, [0]; code that starts at index 1 may index past the end.
A power of two: the new top bit appears and the count falls back to 1 at index 16.
2001 results: a per-number bit loop does over twenty thousand operations, while the dp-on-i>>1 version does one per entry.

hints.text: How are the set bits of i related to those of i halved (dropping its last bit)?
Reuse earlier answers: bits(i) = bits(i >> 1) plus the lowest bit of i. That fills the whole array in one pass with no per-number bit loop.

result[0] = 0
for i from 1 to n:
  result[i] = result[i shifted right by 1] + (i AND 1)
return result

cases.note: One element gives exactly two subsets: [] and [0]. Don't forget the empty set.
Same values as example 1 in another order: subsets and their elements may come back in any order.
0 is a normal element here: its subsets must not be dropped by a truthiness check.
Nine numbers give 512 subsets; the result must contain every one exactly once.

hints.text: For each element there are two choices. How many different results do n independent choices give?

Build subsets incrementally: start with the empty set, and for each new number copy every existing subset and add the number to the copy. Alternatively use backtracking: include it, recurse, then exclude it.

cases.note: One interval has nothing to merge with: return it as is.
Intervals that only touch at an endpoint (4) still merge into [1, 5].
Nothing overlaps, but the input is in reverse: the output must be sorted by start.
Zero-length intervals at 0 that are identical: they collapse into a single [0, 0].
400 chained intervals given in reverse that all fuse into [0, 400]: repeated pairwise merging is cubic.

hints.text: If the intervals were ordered by start, which neighbours could possibly overlap?

Sort by start. Keep the last merged interval; if the next one starts at or before its end, stretch that end to the larger of the two ends, otherwise begin a new interval. Touching endpoints count as overlapping.

cases.note: A null head: there is nothing to reverse, and head.next would throw.
A lone node is its own reverse; make sure its next stays null.
Identical values: the output looks the same either way, so only a correct pointer flip (no lost or repeated nodes) gets the full length.
Zero values: checking if (head.val) instead of if (head) stops early.
3000 nodes: a recursive reversal gets deep, and a quadratic one gets slow.

hints.text: Every next pointer currently faces forward. What must you remember before you flip one of them, so the rest of the list isn't lost?
Walk the list once, keeping a 'previous' node that starts as null. At each node, save its next, point it back at previous, then step both forward. When you run off the end, previous is the new head.

previous = null
current = head
while current is not null:
  following = current.next
  current.next = previous
  previous = current
  current = following
return previous

cases.note: Both heads are null: the answer is the empty list, and you must not touch .val.
One list is empty: the other must be returned as is.
Same as above with the empty list on the right.
Every comparison ties: using < in place of <= still works, but dropping nodes on a tie does not.
Every node of the first list goes before the second: the tail of the loop must attach the leftovers.
The second list entirely precedes the first.
800 nodes per list: building the merge recursively gets deep, and re-scanning for the minimum gets slow.

hints.text: Both lists are already sorted. At any moment, which single node is the next one that has to go into the answer?
Keep a pointer into each list and a dummy head for the result. Repeatedly attach the smaller front node and advance that list; when one list runs out, attach the whole remainder of the other.

dummy = new node
tail = dummy
while a is not null and b is not null:
  if a.value <= b.value:
    tail.next = a
    a = a.next
  else:
    tail.next = b
    b = b.next
  tail = tail.next
tail.next = (a if a is not null else b)
return dummy.next

cases.note: One node whose next is null: the fast pointer's next.next must be guarded.
An empty list has no cycle; head is null so head.next would throw.
A single node that points to itself.
The tail loops back to itself, so the cycle is only one node long.
Equal values but no loop: comparing values instead of node identity would say true.
Equal values and a real loop: only node identity tells the nodes apart.
A long list with the loop in the middle: a solution that counts steps up to a fixed limit gives up too early.
1000 identical values and no cycle: value comparison reports a cycle that isn't there.

hints.text: If the list has no end, walking forward forever never reaches null. How could you notice that you are going around in circles?

Two pointers: a slow one moving one step and a fast one moving two. Inside a loop the fast pointer must eventually lap the slow one and land on the same node; if the fast one reaches null, there is no cycle. This needs O(1) extra space.

slow = head
fast = head
while fast is not null and fast.next is not null:
  slow = slow.next
  fast = fast.next.next
  if slow is the same node as fast:
    return true
return false

cases.note: The only node is the middle: the answer is the whole one-node list.
Even length with two nodes: the middle is the second node, not the first.
All values tie, so only the node you return (second middle, giving two nodes) reveals an off-by-one.
Zeros as data: tests that truthiness isn't used to decide whether to keep walking.
The maximum of 100 nodes, even length: the answer starts at 51 and runs to the end.

hints.text: If you knew the length, how many steps from the head would the middle node be? Can you find it without measuring the list first?

Run two pointers from the head: one moves one node at a time, the other two. When the fast pointer can't go any further, the slow one is at the middle. With an even count this lands on the second of the two middle nodes, which is what is asked.

slow = head
fast = head
while fast is not null and fast.next is not null:
  slow = slow.next
  fast = fast.next.next
return slow

cases.note: Removing the only node leaves an empty list: the answer is null, and a missing dummy node breaks here.
n equals the length, so the head itself is deleted.
n = 1 removes the tail: the trailing pointer must stop at the second-to-last node.
Two nodes, delete the head.
Equal values: deleting 'a node with this value' by value, rather than by position, goes wrong.
A zero is removed from the middle; zero is not a null to stop on.
Maximum size (30 nodes) with n = 30: the lead pointer has to walk all the way to the end before the trail starts.

hints.text: The n-th node from the end is length - n steps from the front. How could you locate it in a single pass, without knowing the length?

Use two pointers n nodes apart. Advance the lead pointer n steps, then move both until the lead falls off the end: the trailing pointer now sits just before the node to delete. A dummy node in front handles deleting the head.

dummy = new node pointing at head
lead = dummy
trail = dummy
repeat n times:
  lead = lead.next
while lead.next is not null:
  lead = lead.next
  trail = trail.next
trail.next = trail.next.next
return dummy.next

cases.note: 0 + 0 must come back as the single digit 0, not an empty list.
One digit each and a carry out of the last column: the answer grows by a node ([0,1]).
Lists of different length, and the carry ripples through every digit of the longer one.
One operand is zero: the other must pass through unchanged.
Repeated 9s: the carry has to be added again at each node, not just once.
A 100-digit number: converting to a JS Number loses precision, and the carry travels through 100 nodes.

hints.text: The digits are stored least significant first, which is the order you'd add them on paper. What do you need to carry from one column to the next?

Walk both lists together, adding the two current digits plus the carry. Emit sum % 10, carry floor(sum / 10). Keep going while either list has digits left or the carry is non-zero, treating a missing digit as 0. Don't convert to a number: 100 digits overflow.

dummy = new node
tail = dummy
carry = 0
while l1 is not null or l2 is not null or carry > 0:
  total = carry
  if l1 is not null: total = total + l1.value, l1 = l1.next
  if l2 is not null: total = total + l2.value, l2 = l2.next
  tail.next = new node(total mod 10)
  tail = tail.next
  carry = total div 10
return dummy.next

cases.note: A single node reads the same both ways: the answer is true.
Two equal nodes: the smallest even-length palindrome.
Odd length: the middle node must be skipped, and it must not be compared with itself or with a neighbour.
Contains zeros but is not a palindrome: the zero check must not make it look symmetric.
3000 nodes that mirror perfectly: a recursive or quadratic approach gets deep or slow.
Mirrors perfectly except one node just past the middle: only a full comparison of both halves catches it.

hints.text: A palindrome reads the same from both ends, but a singly-linked list only lets you walk forward. What would let you read the back half in reverse?

Find the middle with slow and fast pointers, reverse the second half in place, then walk the first half and the reversed half together comparing values. That is O(n) time and O(1) extra space (copying values to an array is O(n) space).

find middle with slow and fast pointers
(for odd length, step slow once more)
second = reverse the list starting at slow
left = head
while second is not null:
  if left.value != second.value: return false
  left = left.next
  second = second.next
return true

cases.note: A null head: there is nothing to remove, and dummy-less code dereferences null.
Every node matches, so the result is empty and the head has to move several times.
Consecutive matches at the head: a single 'if head matches' check removes only one.
The match is the tail: the previous node's next must become null.
Adjacent matches in the middle: after unlinking one, the new next may match too.
The target value is 0, which is falsy: write val === target, not a truthiness test.
3000 nodes with many matches: recursion gets deep, and deleting by re-scanning from the head gets slow.

hints.text: Deleting a node means the node before it must skip over it. What if the node you need to delete is the head, which has nothing before it?

Put a dummy node in front of the head so every real node has a predecessor. Walk with a pointer to the predecessor: if the next node holds the value, link past it (and stay put, since the new next could match too); otherwise move forward.

cases.note: An empty tree must come back empty: root.left on null throws.
Only a left child exists; it has to end up on the right, with the left slot becoming empty.
Equal values hide a swap that forgot to move a subtree: only the shape reveals it.
A 400-deep left chain: it must become a right chain, and recursion goes 400 levels down.

hints.text: Look at a single node with two children. What would the mirror image of just that node and its two subtrees look like?
Mirroring the whole tree means swapping the two children at every node. Do it recursively (swap, then handle each subtree) or with a queue or stack, visiting every node exactly once.

if root is empty: return empty
swap root.left and root.right
invert the subtree now in root.left
invert the subtree now in root.right
return root

cases.note: An empty tree has depth 0, not 1 and not an error.
A lone node has depth 1: count nodes on the path, not edges.
Values are irrelevant to depth; negative values must not leak into the answer.
A 600-deep right chain: the answer is the node count.

hints.text: If you already knew the depth of the left subtree and of the right subtree, what would the depth of the whole tree be?
The depth of a node is one more than the deeper of its two children, and an empty tree has depth 0. A recursive DFS expresses that directly; a level-by-level BFS that counts levels works too.

if root is empty: return 0
leftDepth = depth of root.left
rightDepth = depth of root.right
return 1 + max(leftDepth, rightDepth)

cases.note: Both trees empty: they are the same. Reading .val on null throws.
Exactly one tree is empty: a check like p.val === q.val dereferences null.
Same values, different shape: comparing level-order values while ignoring empty slots says equal.
Two identical 330-deep chains: every level matches until the very bottom.
Identical except the deepest node: an early-exit shortcut on the top levels will say true.

hints.text: Two trees match when their roots match and what hangs off each root matches. What are all the ways a single pair of positions can disagree?
Walk both trees in lockstep. Two empty spots match, exactly one empty spot is a mismatch, and two real nodes must have equal values and then match on both the left pair and the right pair.

if p and q are both empty: return true
if exactly one is empty: return false
if p.val differs from q.val: return false
return same(p.left, q.left) and same(p.right, q.right)

cases.note: A tree with only a root is symmetric: there is nothing to compare.
A left child with no matching right child: not symmetric.
Every value is 2 and the nodes are symmetric in count, but not in shape: both subtrees hang to the same side.
Mirrored pair of equal negative values with their children on opposite sides: symmetric.
A left-only chain is never symmetric; recursion goes 300 levels before the first mismatch surfaces.

hints.text: Cover the right half of the tree and mirror the left half across the middle. Which pairs of nodes have to match?
Compare two subtrees at a time: the left child of one with the right child of the other, and the right child of one with the left child of the other. Start with the root's two children.

check(a, b):
  if a and b are both empty: return true
  if exactly one is empty: return false
  if a.val differs from b.val: return false
  return check(a.left, b.right) and check(a.right, b.left)
answer = check(root.left, root.right)

cases.note: An empty tree gives an empty list, not [[]].
Every level holds exactly one node: 300 levels of one-element arrays.
9 levels with up to 256 values in the last: wrong grouping or an O(n^2) array shift shows here.

hints.text: Which data structure hands you nodes in the order they were discovered, so that all nodes at one depth come out before any at the next?
Run a BFS with a queue. At each round, note how many nodes are in the queue right now: those are exactly one level. Pop that many, record their values, and push their children for the next round.

if root is empty: return empty list
queue = [root]
result = empty list
while queue is not empty:
  size = number of items in queue
  level = empty list
  repeat size times:
    node = remove front of queue
    add node.val to level
    push node.left and node.right if they exist
  add level to result
return result

cases.note: A single node is a valid BST.
Equal values are not allowed on either side: left must be strictly smaller, right strictly larger.
A left child equal to its parent is invalid; a check using <= on the wrong side accepts it.
Values at the 32-bit limits: a sentinel like -2147483648 as the initial bound wrongly rejects the root.
Right child -1 is smaller than the 0 root. Falsy-0 checks on a bound can skip this comparison.
A strictly increasing 600-deep right chain is a valid BST.
Only the very last node (300 levels down) breaks the ordering, against an ancestor far above its parent.

hints.text: Is it enough that each node is bigger than its left child and smaller than its right child? Picture a node deep in the left subtree of the root.

Every node must fit inside a window of allowed values inherited from all its ancestors, with strict inequalities. Going left shrinks the upper bound, going right raises the lower bound. Alternatively, an in-order walk must be strictly increasing.

check(node, low, high):
  if node is empty: return true
  if node.val <= low or node.val >= high: return false
  return check(node.left, low, node.val)
     and check(node.right, node.val, high)
start with low = minus infinity, high = plus infinity

cases.note: One node: the longest path has zero edges, so the answer is 0, not 1.
A 600-node chain: the diameter is its full length in edges (599) and one end is the root.
Perfect tree of depth 9: the diameter bends at the root. An O(n^2) height-per-node approach is slow here.

hints.text: The longest path has a single highest node where it bends. If you knew that node, how would you compute the path length through it?

For every node, the longest path bending there equals height(left) + height(right), counting edges. Compute heights bottom-up, and update a running best at each node while you do it, so one DFS is enough.

best = 0
height(node):
  if node is empty: return 0
  l = height(node.left)
  r = height(node.right)
  best = max(best, l + r)
  return 1 + max(l, r)
height(root)
return best

cases.note: An empty tree has no root-to-leaf path at all, so even a target of 0 is false.
The root alone sums to 1, but it is not a leaf: the path has to run down to node 2.
Negative values and a negative target: you can't stop early because the running sum overshoots.
The root itself sums to 0 but is not a leaf; the real paths sum to 1.
A 500-node chain whose full sum (1+2+...+500) is the target: the path ends at the very bottom.
Only the all-right path 1+3+7+...+255 reaches 502, so every other branch must be explored and rejected.

hints.text: After you step from the root into a child, what target should the rest of the path be aiming for?

Subtract each node's value from the target as you descend. A path counts only if it ends at a leaf (a node with no children), so succeed exactly when you stand on a leaf and the remaining target equals its value.

if root is empty: return false
remaining = targetSum - root.val
if root has no children: return remaining == 0
return hasPathSum(root.left, remaining)
    or hasPathSum(root.right, remaining)

cases.note: k equals the node count: the answer is the largest value, the last node of the in-order walk.
k = 1 is the leftmost leaf, one level below the root.
The smallest value is 0: returning a falsy result, or using 0 as 'not found', breaks here.
A 600-deep left chain: the smallest value is at the very bottom.

hints.text: A binary search tree has a natural way to visit its values from smallest to largest. Which traversal is it?

An in-order walk (left subtree, node, right subtree) visits values in ascending order. Count nodes as you visit them and stop at the k-th one; an explicit stack lets you stop early without collecting everything.

stack = empty
node = root
repeat:
  while node is not empty:
    push node on stack
    node = node.left
  node = pop from stack
  k = k - 1
  if k == 0: return node.val
  node = node.right

cases.note: An empty tree has an empty view.
Only a left child: from the right it is still the node you see on level 2.
The deepest level has only a left node. It is the visible one there; taking only right children misses it.
A left-only 400-deep chain: every node is visible, even though no node has a right child.

hints.text: Standing to the right of the tree, which single node at each depth would you see?

At each depth, the visible node is the last one in left-to-right order. A level-by-level BFS makes that the last node of each level; a DFS that visits right before left sees the first node it reaches at each new depth.

if root is empty: return empty list
queue = [root]
view = empty list
while queue is not empty:
  size = number of items in queue
  repeat size times:
    node = remove front of queue
    remember node as last
    push node.left, node.right if they exist
  add last.val to view
return view
